newsitem.title: MEXICO: Key facts about Mexico's July 6 national elections.
newsitem.headline: Key facts about Mexico's July 6 national elections.

text.p: Mexicans vote on Sunday in crucial mid-term congressional and governors' elections that may see the governing Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) lose its grip on power for the first time in 68 years.
Following are key facts about the July 6 national and governors' election:
-- 52.2 million Mexicans are registered to vote.

-- Three main parties are contesting the elections: the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), the conservative National Action Party (PAN), and the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD).

-- The Workers' Party (PT), the Green Ecologist Party of Mexico (PVEM) and other small parties are also putting up candidates. They must win at least 2 percent of the national vote or an electoral district outright to gain representation.
-- Under Mexico's constitution, the lower house has exclusive responsibility for approving the federal budget and instigating criminal proceedings against corrupt officials.
-- The PRI has controlled both houses of congress since the party was founded in 1929.
-- All 500 seats in the lower house (the Chamber of Deputies) are being contested for three-year terms. The house's composition is as follows: 302 PRI, 118 PAN, 70 PRD, 10 PT.

-- 300 deputies will be elected in a first-past-the-post system from 300 electoral districts across the country. In the last elections in 1994, the PRI won 275 of the 300 districts, the PAN 19 and the PRD 6.
-- The other 200 deputies will be elected by proportional representation from regional party lists.

-- If one party wins over 42 percent of the national vote for the Chamber of Deputies, but fails to win the 251 electoral districts it would need for an overall majority, the difference will be made up to a majority by proportional representation under a so-called "governability clause".

-- No one party is allowed to win more than 60 percent of the seats, regardless of its vote. This is to ensure that constitutional changes, which require a two-thirds majority, can only occur with the consent of the opposition.

-- A quarter (32) of the Senate's 128 seats will also be contested. The Senate's current composition is as follows: 95 PRI, 25 PAN, 8 PRD. Of the 32 seats being contested, 31 are held by the PRI and one by the PAN.
-- The 32 senators will be chosen by proportional representation from a single national list of party candidates.
-- The PRI's 68-year-old Senate majority is not at risk, since even if it lost all the 31 seats it currently holds, it would still have half the Upper Chamber.
-- Mexicans also elect governors in Campeche, Colima, Nuevo Leon, San Luis Potosi, Sonora and Queretaro states. All these governorships are currently held by the PRI.
